title: Window air conditioner: safe teardown
summary: A working window unit is worth more whole: it cools and dries a room (small units draw roughly 500–1,000 W, big 230 V ones over 1,500 W). From a dead one take the two-shaft fan motor with its blower wheel and fan, the run capacitor, the control board and temperature sensors, and the cord. The dangers are the sealed refrigerant loop (flammable on some newer units), a capacitor that holds a charge after unplugging, and a heavy, awkward lift out of the window.

steps.text: Decide first. If it still cools, keep it whole: it can run from a generator or an inverter big enough for the watts and amps on its rating plate. Read the plate (on the side, or behind the front cover: unplug the unit before you open anything) for volts and refrigerant. R-22 and R-410A don't burn. R-32 and R-290 do, as does any refrigerant behind a flammable-refrigerant label or red-marked tubing.
steps.warn: With a flammable refrigerant, keep flames, sparks and cigarettes away for the whole job. Refrigerant may have no smell, so don't trust your nose. Hissing or oily stains mean the loop is already open: step back, air the area and read safety_refrigerant.

steps.text: Unplug it and keep the plug where you can see it. If a generator or inverter was feeding it, switch that off too. If there is no plug because the unit is wired into the wall, don't open it: switch its breaker off, tag it and prove the wiring dead first (safety_mains_isolation). From now on wait at least 5 minutes before you reach inside the case.

If it is still in a window, take it out with a helper. Work from inside the room and never lean out of the window: leave any outside bracket you can't reach from inside. Have your helper take the unit's weight with both hands before you undo the last screw or bracket that fixes it to the sash and frame. Fold the side curtains in, raise the sash and prop it open with a block so it can't drop on your hands, then lift the unit level into the room together. Water left in the base pan will spill, so lay a towel and a bucket ready. Don't tilt the unit outwards to drain it while it sits on the sill.
steps.warn: Friedrich's units weigh 65–75 lb (29–34 kg), and a 230 V Hisense 110 lb (50 kg). Once the sash is up only your hands hold it: it can tip out and kill someone below, or pull you out after it. Keep everyone clear below. If two of you can't hold it, leave it. Wear gloves: the coil fins cut.

steps.text: Set it on a firm bench or the floor, outdoors or in an airy room. Look into the blower and the base pan. If you see black or furry growth, put on a dust mask (P2 or N95) and gloves and keep them on for the rest of the job.

Take off the front grille and filter: usually one to four screws, then the grille lifts off its tabs. Then undo the screws that hold the outer case to the base pan and lift the case off. Some units instead slide out of a separate wall sleeve.
steps.warn: Don't touch anything inside yet: the run capacitor may still be charged. The sheet-metal edges and coil fins are sharp.

steps.text: Find the run capacitor in the control area: a metal or plastic can, often held by a strap, usually with three terminal groups marked C (or COM), HERM and FAN. Clip your resistor tool's lead to C and hold the probe on HERM, then on FAN, for at least 10 seconds each. Then clip the lead to bare chassis metal and touch each terminal in turn (see safety_discharge_capacitor). If the capacitor has only two terminals, or there is more than one, do every one the same way. If large cylindrical capacitors sit on a circuit board that drives the compressor (an inverter model), read the motor-drive section of safety_discharge_capacitor before you touch that board.
steps.warn: Never short it with a screwdriver: many motor capacitors are internally fused and shorting can ruin them, and the arc can burn you. Friedrich says a motor's start terminal on a 230 V circuit can reach as high as 400 V while running: treat the capacitor as live until the meter reads under 1 V.

steps.text: Prove it is empty. Check your meter on a known source, set it to DC volts and measure C to HERM, C to FAN, and each terminal to chassis. You want under 1 V. Check the meter on the known source again. Then clip a jumper wire across all the terminals and leave it there while you work.
steps.warn: If any reading stays above 1 V, discharge again and measure again.

steps.text: Photograph the wiring and put a tape label on every wire before you pull any plug or connector.

Take the control parts. Undo the screws holding the control or relay board, pull each plug by its housing, and lift the board out. Unclip the temperature sensors (small beads on thin leads, clipped to a coil or sitting in the air stream) and take any small transformer. On an older unit with a dial thermostat, follow its thin sensing tube from the thermostat body and unclip it only if it comes free.
steps.warn: Some thin tubes are refrigerant lines and look alike. Never cut, kink or pull any tube you can't trace back to the thermostat body.

steps.text: Take the capacitor out: pull its spade connectors, undo its strap, and twist a bare wire across its terminals before you store it.

Take the outdoor fan off the motor shaft. Some are held by a spring clamp on the hub, which comes off with pliers; others by a set screw. Then reach through the blower housing and free the indoor blower wheel the same way.
steps.warn: Never lever against a coil or tube to free a stuck fan: a nicked or bent tube can split and spray refrigerant and oil. Soak a rusted hub with penetrating oil and wait.

steps.text: Unplug the fan motor's leads, undo its mounting screws or bracket, and lift it out between the coils. If a shroud or air guide is in the way, unscrew that first.
steps.warn: If the motor won't come out without bending tubing, leave it where it is.

steps.text: At the compressor (the black steel can low in the base), lift off the terminal cover, pull the leads and the overload protector off its three pins, and keep them together with a label. Leave the compressor and every tube sealed.
steps.warn: Never cut, drill, saw, unbraze or heat a line, and keep grinders and torches away. A cut line sprays refrigerant and oil: frostbite, eye injury, and fire with R-32 or R-290. R-410A runs at about 60% higher pressure than R-22.

steps.text: Only as a last resort, and only if you really need the compressor: the crimp-first method in teardown_fridge_compressor was written for fridges, not window units. Work outdoors and, with a flammable refrigerant, away from any flame or spark. Do it only if both lines at the compressor are copper no thicker than 1/2 in (12.7 mm) outside, and you have a pinch-off tool made for that size. Otherwise leave it.
steps.warn: Don't use locking pliers: they may not seal tubing this size at this pressure. Friedrich's SQ08N10 holds 22 oz (624 g) of R-410A, which runs about 60% higher pressure than R-22. Wear goggles and gloves. If a crimp hisses or weeps oil, don't cut: step back and let it vent outdoors, away from flames.

steps.text: Cut the cord off where it enters the case and keep it whole with its plug. Keep the case and base pan for sheet steel.

notes:
## What's worth keeping and why

- **The working unit.** Best of all. Friedrich's Q-chassis models draw 514–969 W when cooling at 115 V and also pull water out of the air (Friedrich Q manual). Size a generator or inverter from the plate, with headroom for the compressor's start.
- **Fan motor, blower wheel and fan.** One permanent split capacitor (PSC) motor drives both the indoor blower and the outdoor fan, and has a self-resetting overload inside (Friedrich Q manual). The GoldStar GWHD6500R's is a 6-pole, 28 W, two-speed motor with a turbo blower inside and a propeller fan with a slinger ring outside (GoldStar GWHD6500R manual). Use it, with its run capacitor, for shelter ventilation, drying or a forge blower wherever mains power exists.
- **Run capacitor.** The Friedrich SQ08N10 uses a dual 45/7.5 µF, 370 V capacitor (Friedrich Q manual). It is a spare for any motor or compressor that calls for the same values (test_capacitor).
- **Control board.** Friedrich's relay board switches the fan speeds, has 5 V and 3.3 V test points and a T3.15 A, 250 V fuse (Friedrich Q manual). Its relays switch mains loads; its fuse is a spare.
- **Temperature sensors.** Friedrich's thermistors read 10.0 kΩ at 25 °C (77 °F) and 26.05 kΩ at 0 °C (32 °F) (Friedrich Q manual): ready-made sensors for a microcontroller thermometer or thermostat.
- **Compressor overload.** The Friedrich's sits outside the compressor and senses both current and winding heat; it can take minutes to hours to reset (Friedrich Q manual). Keep it with its compressor.
- **Cord.** Many newer units have a plug with TEST and RESET buttons (an LCDI). It senses damage to its own cord and is not an on/off switch (Friedrich Q manual; Frigidaire use & care). The Friedrich's plug is a 125 V, 15 A NEMA 5-15P (Friedrich Q manual). Don't count on the plug as an RCD or GFCI for anything else.
- **Sheet steel.** The case and base pan: brackets, guards, heat shields.

## Testing what you got out

- **Fan motor.** Friedrich's test, with the capacitor connected: power on the black lead and the capacitor's common terminal runs high speed, the red lead runs low (Friedrich Q manual). Lead colours vary by maker, so follow the motor label or the unit's wiring diagram. Bench-test only through an RCD or GFCI, with the terminals covered and the fan and blower off the shaft or guarded.
- **Capacitor.** See test_capacitor. Test both halves of a dual capacitor (Friedrich Q manual).
- **Thermistors.** On the ohms range at room temperature a 10 kΩ type reads near 10 kΩ, and the reading drops as you warm it in your hand.
- **Overload.** Continuity at room temperature only shows it is closed. It can't show it will still open when it should: never heat it to test it, never bridge it, and never make a salvaged one the only protection.

## Variations

- **GoldStar GWHD6500R (2005).** R-22, 380 g (13.4 oz), capillary-tube metering and thermistor control. The front grille comes off after one screw and lifts out of tabs; the case comes off after nine screws. GoldStar says to discharge the capacitor through a 20 kΩ resistor, and to recover the refrigerant before unbrazing the compressor (GoldStar GWHD6500R manual).
- **Friedrich SQ08N10 (2012 series).** R-410A, 22.0 oz (624 g). The Q-chassis models weigh 65–75 lb (29–34 kg) and Friedrich says to use two people to lift or carry one. The front cover comes off after 4 screws (Friedrich Q manual).
- **Newer flammable-refrigerant units.** Frigidaire's 2019 manual names R-32 and says it must be recovered, not released into the air (Frigidaire use & care). GE's AWES06 warns of fire or explosion, says not to drill holes in the unit or pierce the tubing, that refrigerants may have no smell, and recommends two people for installing it (GE AWES06 manual). The EPA notes that hydrocarbon refrigerant is marked by a warning label and red tubing (EPA disaster guidance).
- **Heat and bigger units.** Some models add an electric heating element; Friedrich's EQ08N11 is one (Friedrich Q manual). On an old unit, look for asbestos (grey or white fibrous board, rope seals, papery wrap) before you handle an element, insulation or gaskets, and leave it if unsure (safety_asbestos_check). Larger units run on 230 V and weigh more. Hisense's 18,000 BTU AW1822DR3W takes 230 V and 20 A on a NEMA 6-20P plug, weighs 50 kg (110 lb) net and holds 630 g of R-32 (Hisense AW1822DR3W spec). Its inverter-driven AW1823TW3W takes 230 V and 15 A on a 6-15P plug, weighs 39 kg (86 lb) net and holds 550 g of R-32 (Hisense AW1823TW3W spec). A plug-in 230 V unit is still made safe by unplugging it, but plan a bigger lift, a bigger flammable charge and, on an inverter model, the drive board's capacitors.

## What to leave

- **The sealed loop:** compressor, both coils, the capillary tube, the drier and every tube between them. Only take a compressor by the crimp-first method, and only where it fits the limits in the steps. Yellow Jacket's bar-style pinch-off tool, for example, is made for 1/4 to 1/2 in copper (Yellow Jacket brochure).
- **Releasing refrigerant on purpose.** In the US it is illegal to knowingly vent it when getting rid of a window air conditioner, and recovery needs EPA-certified recovery equipment (EPA disaster guidance). Friedrich's service manual likewise says to recover the refrigerant before opening the system (Friedrich Q manual).
- **Coils for their copper and aluminium:** only from a unit whose loop is already broken (safety_refrigerant).
- The plastic front and the foam seals.
